analogy.p: Imagine a tug of war. Each team pulls with a force, and the winner is decided by the resultant of the two teams' forces: equal pulls give a stalemate (resultant zero, the rope does not accelerate), while a stronger team produces a resultant towards their side and the rope speeds up that way. The rope is the 'object' and the free body diagram shows only the two pulls on the rope. The analogy breaks down because in real tug of war the ground friction on the players is also crucial, and it only describes forces in a straight line, not forces at angles.

bullets: **Resultant force** = the single force that can replace all the forces acting on an object and have the same effect on its motion.
Force is a **vector** quantity (it has magnitude AND direction), so directions matter when adding forces.
The resultant is measured in **newtons (N)**.
The resultant force is what appears in **F = m a**: it is the resultant force, not just any one force, that causes acceleration.
If the resultant is zero the forces are **balanced**; if it is not zero the forces are **unbalanced**.
Resultant force can change the **speed**, the **direction**, or the **shape** of an object.
Link to other topics: scalar and vector quantities (4.5.1.1), Newton's laws (4.5.3).
core.p: A **resultant force** is the single force that has the **same effect** as all the original forces acting on an object together. Real objects almost always have more than one force on them: a car feels a driving force, drag, weight and a reaction force from the road. Instead of tracking every force, we add them up (taking direction into account) to get one number and one direction. That single force is what decides how the object's motion changes. If you can find the resultant, you can predict the motion.

bullets: **Same direction:** add. A 4 N push and a 3 N push both to the right give a resultant of 7 N to the right.
**Opposite directions:** subtract the smaller from the larger. 5 N right and 3 N left gives 2 N to the right.
The resultant acts in the direction of the **larger** force.
With three or more forces: add all those one way, add all those the other way, then subtract.
Always state the **direction** with the size, for example '2 N to the right'.
Always include the **unit (N)**.
Example: driving force 900 N forwards, drag 400 N backwards, friction 100 N backwards gives 900 - 400 - 100 = 400 N forwards.
core.h: Adding forces in a straight line
core.p: When forces act along the same straight line, you add the ones that point the same way and subtract the ones that point the opposite way. Choose one direction as positive (for example right), treat the opposite direction as negative, then add up all the forces. The sign of the answer tells you the direction of the resultant. This works because forces in the same direction reinforce each other, while forces in opposite directions partly cancel.

bullets: Balanced forces: resultant = **0 N**, so acceleration = **0 m/s²**.
A stationary object with balanced forces stays at rest.
A moving object with balanced forces keeps moving at **constant velocity** (same speed AND same direction).
A car at a steady 30 m/s on a flat road has driving force = drag (resultant 0).
A skydiver at terminal velocity has weight = air resistance.
A book on a table has weight (down) = normal contact force (up).
Balanced does not mean no forces: there can be large forces that cancel exactly.
core.p: If the forces on an object are balanced the resultant force is **0 N**. The object then behaves exactly as if no force were acting. A stationary object stays stationary, and a moving object carries on at the **same speed in a straight line** (constant velocity). This is Newton's first law. It is a very common mistake to think a moving object needs a resultant force to keep moving: it does not, it only needs a resultant force to change its velocity.

bullets: Resultant in the **same direction** as motion: object **speeds up**.
Resultant in the **opposite direction** to motion: object **slows down**.
Resultant at **right angles** to motion: direction changes (for example circular motion at constant speed).
From **F = m a**: a = F / m, so a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration for the same resultant force.
Acceleration is always in the **same direction as the resultant force**.
A stationary object with an unbalanced resultant starts to move in the direction of the resultant.
Unbalanced forces can also change the **shape** of an object (stretching, squashing, bending).
core.p: When the resultant force is **not zero** the forces are unbalanced and the velocity of the object changes. A resultant force in the direction of motion makes the object speed up, a resultant force opposite to the motion makes it slow down (decelerate), and a resultant force at an angle to the motion changes its direction. The bigger the resultant force, the bigger the acceleration, and the bigger the mass, the smaller the acceleration for the same force. The link is F = m a.

bullets: Draw **only the one object** (a box, circle or dot), not its surroundings.
Draw **only forces acting ON that object**, not forces it exerts on something else.
Each force is an **arrow**: the arrow shows the **direction**, and its **length** shows the relative size.
Start each arrow at the object and point it **away from the object** in the direction the force acts.
Label every arrow with the **name of the force** (weight, normal contact force, drag, friction, thrust, tension, air resistance).
**Balanced** forces give opposite arrows of **equal length**.
An unbalanced diagram has a longer arrow on one side, showing the direction of the resultant.
core.h: Free body diagrams: what they are
core.p: A **free body diagram** shows a **single object** on its own, drawn as a simple box or dot, with **only the forces that act on that object** drawn as arrows. It leaves out everything else: the ground, other objects and the forces the object exerts on other things. Free body diagrams make it much easier to spot the resultant force because you can see every force that acts on the object at a glance. They are a standard exam tool for explaining motion.

bullets: **Weight (W = m g)**: downwards, non-contact force, due to gravity.
**Normal contact force (reaction, R)**: perpendicular to the surface, pushing the object away from the surface.
**Friction**: along the surface, opposite to the direction of motion or attempted motion.
**Drag / air resistance / water resistance**: opposite to the direction of motion through a fluid.
**Thrust / driving force**: in the direction of travel.
**Tension**: along a rope or string, pulling on the object.
**Upthrust**: upwards on an object in a fluid.
Do not draw 'force of motion' or 'momentum' as a force: they are not forces.
core.p: Exam questions use a small set of forces again and again, so learn which way each acts. **Weight** always acts straight down towards the centre of the Earth because it is caused by gravity. The **normal contact force** (also called the reaction force) is a contact force from a surface pushing at right angles to the surface. Resistive forces such as **friction**, **drag** and **air resistance** always act in the direction **opposite to the motion** (or opposite to the way the object would move). Driving forces such as **thrust** or **engine force** act in the direction of travel.

bullets: Step 1: list every force and its direction.
Step 2: choose a positive direction (e.g. right and up).
Step 3: add the forces in each direction, using minus signs for the opposite direction.
Step 4: state the resultant with size, direction and unit.
Step 5: if asked for motion, use **a = F / m** or Newton's first law.
A **vertical** resultant of zero means no change in vertical velocity, so the object stays at the same height or moves at constant vertical velocity.
A **horizontal** resultant of zero means constant horizontal velocity.
core.h: Reading a free body diagram to find the resultant
core.p: Once the diagram is drawn you can find the resultant along each direction separately. Look at the horizontal arrows and combine them, then do the same for the vertical arrows. If an object stays at the same height, the vertical forces are balanced (for example weight = normal contact force). The horizontal forces then decide the motion. This two-step method is the key to every resultant force question.

bullets: Book at rest: **W = R**, resultant 0 N.
Car at steady speed: **driving force = drag + friction**, so resultant 0 N, constant velocity.
Car accelerating: driving force **greater than** resistive forces.
Car braking: braking force and resistive forces act backwards, so the car decelerates.
Skydiver at start of jump: weight **greater than** air resistance, so accelerates downwards.
Skydiver at terminal velocity: weight = air resistance, resultant 0 N.
A parachute opens: air resistance suddenly greater than weight, so the skydiver decelerates (see terminal velocity).
core.h: Worked situations: book, car and skydiver
core.p: Three standard cases cover most exam diagrams. A **book on a table** has two forces, weight down and normal contact force up, which are equal, so the resultant is zero and the book stays at rest. A **car moving at constant speed** has driving force equal to drag horizontally, and weight equal to the normal contact force vertically. A **skydiver at terminal velocity** has weight balanced by air resistance. In each case, the forces are balanced, so the velocity is constant.

bullets: Use a **ruler** and **protractor** and pick a sensible scale, for example 1 cm = 1 N.
Draw forces **tail to head** (each new arrow starts where the last one ended).
The resultant joins the **start of the first arrow to the end of the last**.
The order of drawing does not change the resultant.
For forces at right angles: R² = F1² + F2², so R = √(F1² + F2²).
The angle to the first force: tan θ = F2 / F1, so θ = tan⁻¹(F2 / F1).
Give the answer as a **size and a direction** (an angle from a stated line).
Exam answers from scale drawings are accepted within a tolerance, so be neat and accurate.
core.h: Forces not in a straight line (Higher tier)
core.p: When two forces act at an angle to each other you cannot simply add or subtract. In Higher tier you find the resultant using a **scale drawing**: choose a scale, draw the first force as an arrow, draw the second force starting at the **head** (tip) of the first, then draw a line from the start of the first to the end of the second. That line is the **resultant** in both size and direction. Measure it and convert back with your scale. For forces at right angles you can use **Pythagoras** and **trigonometry** instead.

bullets: For a force F at angle θ above the horizontal: **horizontal component = F cos θ**.
**Vertical component = F sin θ**.
Check: (F cos θ)² + (F sin θ)² = F², because cos²θ + sin²θ = 1.
Example: 50 N at 30° gives 50 cos 30° = 43.3 N horizontally and 50 sin 30° = 25 N vertically.
A rope pulling a sledge upwards at an angle: only the **horizontal component** pulls the sledge forwards.
The vertical component reduces the normal contact force on the ground.
Make sure your calculator is in **degree mode**.
On a scale drawing, draw the force, then construct the horizontal and vertical sides of the right-angled triangle and measure them.
core.h: Resolving a force into components (Higher tier)
core.p: Resolving is the reverse of finding a resultant: a **single force** is replaced by **two forces at right angles** that together have the same effect. The two forces are called **components**, usually one horizontal and one vertical. This is useful because the horizontal and vertical motions can be analysed separately. You can do it with a scale drawing (draw the force, then draw a right-angled triangle) or with trigonometry.

bullets: Equilibrium means resultant force = 0 N.
Three forces in equilibrium make a **closed triangle** when drawn tail to head.
Use the closed triangle to find a **missing force** by scale drawing.
The missing force acts in the direction that closes the shape.
A picture hanging from two strings at an angle: tension in both strings and the weight form a closed triangle.
The tensions are greater than half the weight when the strings are at an angle, because only a component of each tension acts upwards.
Equilibrium does not mean at rest: it also includes constant velocity.
core.h: Equilibrium and closed force triangles (Higher tier)
core.p: An object in **equilibrium** has no resultant force on it. If three forces act on an object in equilibrium and you draw them tail to head, the arrows form a **closed triangle**, ending exactly where they started. If the arrows do not close, there is a resultant force. This idea can be used to find an unknown force: draw the known forces to scale and the missing side of the triangle is the third force. With more than three forces the arrows form a closed polygon.

bullets: First law: zero resultant means constant velocity (or rest).
Second law: **F = m a**, where F is the **resultant** force in N, m is mass in kg, a is acceleration in m/s².
Third law pairs act on **different objects**, so they cannot cancel each other.
Work done: only the resultant force changes the kinetic energy.
Terminal velocity: reached when resultant force becomes zero.
Stopping distances: braking force is the resultant that decelerates the car.
Moments: forces can have zero resultant yet still cause rotation if their lines of action differ.
core.h: Linking to Newton's laws, momentum and energy
core.p: Resultant force is the central idea that links the whole forces topic. **Newton's first law**: if the resultant force is zero, the velocity does not change. **Newton's second law**: the acceleration is proportional to the resultant force and inversely proportional to the mass, F = m a. **Newton's third law** is different because its two forces act on **different** objects, so they never appear together on one free body diagram as a pair that cancel. In Higher tier, resultant force equals the rate of change of momentum.

exam: Command word **'State'** or **'Name'** (1 mark): give the forces by name, for example 'weight' and 'normal contact force'.
**'Calculate the resultant force'** (2 marks): 1 mark for adding or subtracting correctly, 1 mark for the answer with unit and direction.
**'Draw a free body diagram'** (2 to 3 marks): one object, arrows labelled, correct directions, and equal lengths for balanced forces.
**'Explain why the car moves at constant speed'** (2 marks): 'the driving force equals the resistive forces' and 'so the resultant force is zero'.
**'Describe the motion'** (2 to 3 marks): link the resultant to a change in velocity, using **'resultant force'** not just 'force'.
A **4 mark** answer needs a clear chain: forces, resultant, effect on acceleration or velocity, and a reason (F = m a).
A **6 mark** extended answer should structure ideas in order, for example starting speed, resultant force at each stage, and final steady speed.
For **scale drawing** (Higher, 3 to 4 marks): state your scale, draw tail to head, measure the resultant, convert back, and give the angle.
For **resolving** (Higher, 2 to 3 marks): write F cos θ or F sin θ, substitute, and give the answer with units.
Use the phrase **'resultant force'** and **'balanced / unbalanced'** exactly, as mark schemes look for them.
Always show the formula **F = m a** and the substitution, as marks are given for method even if the answer is wrong.
Units: force in **N**, mass in **kg**, acceleration in **m/s²**; convert grams to kilograms first.

mistakes.r: A constant velocity means the resultant force is zero. A resultant force is only needed to change velocity.
mistakes.w: A moving object must have a resultant force in the direction of motion.

mistakes.r: There can be several forces, but their resultant is zero.
mistakes.w: Balanced forces means there are no forces.

mistakes.r: Only draw forces acting ON the object being studied.
mistakes.w: Drawing the force of the object on the ground in a free body diagram.

mistakes.r: Subtract them (or use a positive and negative direction) and give the direction of the larger one.
Give size, unit (N) and direction, for example '2 N to the right'.
mistakes.w: Forgetting the unit or direction in the answer.

mistakes.r: Balanced forces must be drawn as equal-length arrows in opposite directions.
mistakes.w: Drawing arrows of different lengths for balanced forces.

mistakes.r: They act on the same object. A third law pair acts on two different objects and is the same type of force.
mistakes.w: Saying weight and normal contact force are a Newton's third law pair.

mistakes.r: Use the correct force names, such as thrust, driving force, friction, drag, weight.
mistakes.w: Labelling an arrow 'momentum' or 'force of motion'.

mistakes.r: For an angle θ above the horizontal, vertical = F sin θ and horizontal = F cos θ.
mistakes.w: Using cos for the vertical component.

mistakes.r: Set it to degrees for GCSE angle questions.

summary: You must know that several forces acting on an object can be replaced by one resultant force with the same effect, calculate the resultant of forces acting along a straight line, and draw free body diagrams showing the forces on a single object. In Higher tier you also add forces at an angle using scale drawings and resolve one force into two components at right angles. It matters because resultant force decides whether an object accelerates (Newton's second law) or stays at constant velocity (Newton's first law).

terms.d: A single force that has the same effect as all the forces acting on an object together.
Forces whose resultant is zero, so there is no change in the object's velocity.
Forces with a non-zero resultant, which cause the object to accelerate.
A diagram of a single object showing only the forces acting on that object, as arrows.
A quantity that has both magnitude and direction, for example force.
The unit of force. One newton gives a mass of 1 kg an acceleration of 1 m/s².
The force acting on an object due to gravity, W = m g, acting downwards.
The force exerted by a surface on an object resting on it, acting at right angles to the surface.
A contact force between surfaces that opposes motion or attempted motion.
A resistive force acting on an object moving through a fluid, opposing the motion.
One of two forces at right angles which together have the same effect as a single force.
Replacing a single force by two forces at right angles (components) that have the same effect.
The state of an object when the resultant force on it is zero.
A drawing of vectors to a chosen scale used to find a resultant or a component.
The rate of change of velocity, a = change in velocity / time, in m/s².

worked.ans: Resultant force = 1500 N forwards; acceleration = 1.25 m/s² forwards.
worked.q: A car of mass 1200 kg has a driving force of 2400 N forwards. Drag and friction together are 900 N backwards. Calculate the resultant force and the car's acceleration. (4 marks)
steps: Use F = m a, so a = F / m.

worked.q: (Higher) Two forces of 6 N and 8 N act at right angles on an object. Calculate the size of the resultant and its angle to the 6 N force. (4 marks)
steps: Forces are at right angles, so use Pythagoras.

worked.ans: Horizontal component = 72.5 N; vertical component = 33.8 N (3 s.f.).
worked.q: (Higher) A child pulls a sledge with a rope using a force of 80 N at 25° above the horizontal. Calculate the horizontal and vertical components of the force. (3 marks)
steps: Horizontal component = F cos θ = 80 × cos 25° = 80 × 0.9063 = 72.5 N.
Vertical component = F sin θ = 80 × sin 25° = 80 × 0.4226 = 33.8 N.
